content: The management of vaginal discharge involves several approaches based on clinical findings and available diagnostic tools. Treatment should be initiated if vaginal discharge is confirmed through a genital examination, or if a speculum or microscopy test yields positive results. In settings where risk assessment is positive or vaginal discharge is confirmed via genital examination, treatment is also recommended. While treating based solely on confirmed vaginal discharge through genital examination is effective, it may be slightly more expensive. However, this approach is favorable in terms of outcomes. In cases where low-sensitivity and low-specificity point-of-care tests are used, or when speculum examinations are performed, treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease may be slightly higher but not necessarily more costly. Health equity considerations reveal disparities in care-seeking behavior and testing. For example, symptomatic African-American women are more likely to be tested for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) than symptomatic white women. In Mumbai, India, poor women disproportionately seek treatment for vaginal discharge, often linked to psychosocial stressors such as spousal abuse and tension. In rural South Africa, limited access to healthcare services has resulted in a high burden of untreated symptomatic and asymptomatic STIs, highlighting the need for mobile clinics to provide out-of-facility STI services. Socioeconomic factors significantly influence STI prevalence. In Brazil, chlamydia is more prevalent among patients in the public health sector compared to the private sector. Illiterate women and those living in rural areas are at higher risk of chlamydia compared to educated women and those in urban areas. In the United States, young women with lower education levels have a lower prevalence of chlamydia and gonorrhea compared to college-educated Black women, who exhibit higher predicted probabilities of these infections. Additionally, bacterial vaginosis, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Trichomonas vaginalis are more common among non-Hispanic African-Americans than white Americans. Barriers to seeking treatment for vaginal discharge include stigma, fear, lack of awareness, and dissatisfaction with previous healthcare experiences. Cost, geographical access, lack of privacy, and unavailability of free medication are also significant deterrents. In some cases, women may not disclose their symptoms even when visiting healthcare facilities. Among female sex workers in Brazil, 49% reported vaginal discharge, but 42% did not seek treatment at healthcare facilities. Many opted for self-medication or private doctors, with only a minority attending public STI clinics or NGO testing centers. The syndromic management approach has been implemented in various settings with mixed results. In Kenya, a syndromic management program reduced STI incidence during its operation but saw an increase after its termination. In Tanzania, a similar program treated over 12,000 people with STI syndromes in two years, with 50–75% of symptomatic individuals utilizing the service. In Peru, the PREVEN Network trained healthcare providers in syndromic management, resulting in significant improvements in STI management in intervention cities compared to control cities. Despite these efforts, gaps in provider knowledge and adherence to guidelines persist. For example, in South Africa, only 61% of cases received syndromic management according to guidelines, and only 19% of patients received all essential STI services. Similar challenges have been observed in Gujarat, India, and Ethiopia. For individuals with vaginal discharge, good clinical practice includes taking a detailed medical and sexual history, performing a thorough physical examination, and offering testing for HIV and syphilis. Treatment should be based on molecular assay results when available, or on rapid point-of-care tests with high sensitivity and specificity. In settings with limited diagnostic resources, treatment may rely on speculum examination findings or syndromic management. In cases of recurrent or persistent vaginal discharge, referral to a center with laboratory capacity for advanced diagnostics is recommended. This includes testing for antimicrobial-resistant infections and seeking specialist assessment when necessary. While microscopy is the most accurate diagnostic tool, its implementation in resource-limited settings may not be cost-effective compared to treating all confirmed cases of vaginal discharge. In summary, the management of vaginal discharge should balance diagnostic accuracy, cost-effectiveness, and accessibility while addressing disparities in care and barriers to treatment.
